title: Preserving game meat
summary: Keep game cold: below 40°F (4°C), and a hanging carcass no more than 2 to 3 days at that. Storage times are in the table. Every other way to keep meat here carries one of two labels: backed by a food-safety agency, or traditional and not agency-verified. None of them makes game ready to eat: cook it to 165°F (74°C) before eating, except deer jerky made exactly by the agency method. Smoke and dry meat only outdoors.
doFirst: Keep the meat cold: a hanging deer at 40°F (4°C) or below for 2 to 3 days at most (Penn State Extension), and never above 45°F (7°C) (NYS Department of Health). Cut meat in a fridge at 40°F (4°C) or below: use it within 1 to 2 days (Utah State University Extension).

Every method on this page keeps meat; none makes it ready to eat. Freezing may not kill trichinella worms in game meat, and curing, drying or smoking alone does not consistently kill them (CDC). Cook it to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part before eating. The one exception is deer jerky made exactly as in “Jerky” below.
Smoke and dry meat outdoors only. Fires and fuel indoors: see Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors.
Don’t make jerky from meat that touched gut contents: cook that meat thoroughly instead (National Center for Home Food Preservation).

blocks.p: Every method below sits under one of two labels, with its source named:

list: Backed by a food-safety agency: the method and its figures come from USDA, FDA, CDC, the National Center for Home Food Preservation, FoodSafety.gov or a state health department.

Traditional: from an extension or historical source, not agency-verified. These are older or simpler ways that an extension service or the US Army survival manual teaches. Each carries its own risk, said plainly, and what the agencies say against it.

blocks.warn: Whatever the label, cook wild game to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part before you eat it, unless the method says otherwise. Use a food thermometer if you have one.

blocks.p: Backed by a food-safety agency (Minnesota Department of Health, FoodSafety.gov). Where an extension service gives a shorter time, the table uses it and names it: those cells are an extension figure, not an agency one. Where sources give different times, use the shorter one. Swipe sideways to see the whole table.

head: Meat
Fridge, 40°F (4°C) or below
Freezer, 0°F (-18°C) or below
rows: 1 to 2 days (Utah State University Extension; Minnesota Department of Health gives 3 to 5)
1 to 2 days (FoodSafety.gov, raw chicken or turkey; Clemson Cooperative Extension gives 3)
6 months (Clemson Cooperative Extension; FoodSafety.gov gives 9 months to 1 year for chicken or turkey)

list: Freezer times are for quality only: frozen food kept continuously at 0°F (-18°C) or below can be kept indefinitely (FoodSafety.gov).

Freeze meat while it is fresh, wrapped tightly with the air pressed out (North Dakota State University Extension, Penn State Extension). Freeze only as much as will freeze solid within 24 hours (North Dakota State University Extension).
Don’t refreeze meat that has thawed (Penn State Extension). What to do with thawed meat after a power cut is in Is it still good?

blocks.p: Backed by a food-safety agency: keep game cool, with ice or below 45°F (7°C), until it is butchered, including a big game carcass hanging for several days (NYS Department of Health).
How long, from the extension services, most cautious first:

list: Penn State Extension: hold the carcass at 40°F (4°C) or below for two to three days, at most. This app goes by this figure.
Cornell Cooperative Extension: keep the deer below 40°F (4°C) while it ages, hung by its hind feet with the skin on. Aging is not needed for tender meat.

North Dakota State University Extension: aging at 34 to 37°F (1 to 3°C) for 10 to 14 days tenderizes meat, but two to three days is enough, and aging is not recommended for a carcass with little or no fat on it, or for meat that will be ground.
New Mexico State University Extension: if the temperature stays at or around 32°F (0°C), venison can age for as long as 10 to 12 days; watch it closely if the day goes above 45°F (7°C).

blocks.p: Put a thermometer where the meat is, so you know the temperature (Kentucky Afield puts one on the ice in a cooler). Warm days or no shade: cut the carcass into quarters and put them on ice (New Mexico State University Extension); cutting up is in Butchering deer and small game.

What the agencies say first. Preserving food quotes New York’s health department: “Don’t put your food outside to keep it cold, even in the winter (New York State Department of Health).” Freezer times assume food kept continuously at 0°F (-18°C) or below (FoodSafety.gov), and Penn State Extension says not to refreeze thawed meat.

Traditional: from a historical source, not agency-verified. The US Army survival manual (FM 21-76, 2006 copy): “In cold climates, you can freeze and keep meat indefinitely.” It goes on: freezing is not a way of preparing meat, and you must still cook it before eating.

list: Its risk, as this app’s caution: outdoor cold is not steady. A sunny day or a warm spell can thaw meat and let it freeze again without your knowing, and animals can get at meat left outside.
North Dakota State University Extension says not to let a whole carcass freeze before it is cut up: freezing may toughen the meat.
End step: cook it to 165°F (74°C) before eating. Freezing does not reliably kill trichinella worms in wild game (CDC).

blocks.p: Backed by a food-safety agency (National Center for Home Food Preservation). This method needs a dehydrator or an oven that holds 140°F (60°C), and a food thermometer. It is for deer: don’t use bear meat for jerky (University of Alaska Fairbanks Extension), which also says to cook bear meat until well done. Jerky from wild boar or any other game is cooked to 165°F (74°C) before eating, as in the end step below. Raw poultry is generally not recommended for jerky (National Center for Home Food Preservation).

steps: Use only meat that was cooled fast and never touched gut contents. If gut contents touched the meat or your hands while dressing it, don’t make jerky from it: use it only in ways that cook it thoroughly (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Partly freeze the meat to make slicing easier. Slice it no thicker than 1/4 inch (6 mm). Trim off and throw away all fat: it turns rancid quickly (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Marinate it covered in the fridge for 1 to 2 hours or overnight (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Heat it before drying: bring the strips and marinade to a boil and boil for 5 minutes. Strips thicker than 1/4 inch may need longer (National Center for Home Food Preservation).

Check several strips with a metal stem thermometer (National Center for Home Food Preservation). For wild game, get them to at least 170°F (77°C). This follows the National Center for Home Food Preservation’s literature review (section 6.4: wild game must be heated to 170°F to destroy trichinella) in place of its jerky page, which heats to 160°F and freezes game first. University of Alaska Fairbanks Extension heats game meat in its marinade to boiling, 212°F (100°C). Both are above the 165°F (74°C) cooking rule for wild game, and USDA’s 160°F (71°C) for meat jerky is not enough for game.
Drain the strips and lay them on racks in a dehydrator or oven preheated to 140°F (60°C) (National Center for Home Food Preservation).
Start checking after 3 hours. It is done when a test piece cracks but does not break when you bend it (National Center for Home Food Preservation).

Store it in a sealed container, glass jars or heavy plastic food bags. Properly dried jerky keeps two weeks at room temperature; refrigerate or freeze it to keep it longer (National Center for Home Food Preservation). Penn State Extension gives one to two months in a fridge below 40°F (4°C).

list: The National Center for Home Food Preservation also freezes pork or wild game first, at 0°F (-18°C) or below for at least 30 days for a piece 6 inches (15 cm) thick or less, to kill trichinella. Do it if you have a freezer, but don’t count on it: freezing may not kill the worms in wild game (CDC). The heat step is the one that counts.
From Preserving food (USDA): “Most dehydrator instructions don’t include this step, and a dehydrator may not reach temperatures high enough to heat meat to 160°F (71.1°C) or 165°F (73.9°C) (USDA).”
Several outbreaks of E. coli O157:H7 have come from venison jerky (National Center for Home Food Preservation).

blocks.p: End step: deer jerky made exactly this way, with the strips checked at 170°F (77°C) before drying, is eaten as it is, within two weeks at room temperature (National Center for Home Food Preservation). Any other jerky, and any jerky you are not sure of: cook it to 165°F (74°C) before eating, for example in a stew.

blocks.warn: Smoke meat outdoors only. From Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors: “Carbon monoxide comes from anything that burns fuel. You cannot see or smell it.”

blocks.label: Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors

blocks.p: Traditional: from an extension source, not agency-verified. North Dakota State University Extension, smoked deer jerky:

steps: Bone out a hind leg and split it into its separate muscles: top, bottom and tip (North Dakota State University Extension).

Make a brine of 2 pounds (0.9 kg) of commercial salt-cure mix per gallon (3.8 L) of water, and pump it into the meat: an ordinary syringe will do, injecting into several places in each muscle (North Dakota State University Extension).

Put the meat in a crock or a food-grade container, never a garbage can, plastic bag or ice cream bucket. Cover it completely with the brine and weight it down so it stays under (North Dakota State University Extension).
Keep it in a cooler at 38°F (3°C) for 10 days, turning the meat and weighting it down again every two days (North Dakota State University Extension).

Take it out of the brine and smoke it for five hours at 150°F (66°C), with hardwood such as hickory, maple, chokecherry, oak or apple; never a soft wood such as pine (North Dakota State University Extension).
Hang it to dry at room temperature, about two weeks (North Dakota State University Extension).

blocks.p: Traditional: from a historical source, not agency-verified. The US Army survival manual (FM 21-76, 2006 copy) smokes meat over a small fire meant to make smoke, not heat, with hardwood and never resinous wood, the meat cut in slices no more than about 2 1/2 inches (6 centimeters, as printed) thick. It says meat smoked overnight lasts about a week, two days of steady smoking preserve it 2 to 4 weeks, and properly smoked meat looks like a dark, curled, brittle stick.

list: Its risk: smoke without proper cooking does not preserve meat (National Center for Home Food Preservation) or kill trichinella (CDC), and 40°F to 140°F (4°C to 60°C) is the range where germs grow (National Center for Home Food Preservation). The North Dakota method smokes at 150°F (66°C), below the 165°F cooking rule; the Army method gives no temperature at all.

What the agencies say: “Smoke itself, without proper cooking, is not an effective food preservative”, and smoking meat at 40°F to 140°F for a long time needs meat salted or cured first (National Center for Home Food Preservation). It gives storage times for smoked meats only in a fridge or freezer. Curing (salting), drying or smoking alone does not consistently kill trichinella worms (CDC).
The Army manual says smoked meat can be eaten without further cooking. This app does not follow that for wild game.
End step: cook smoked meat to 165°F (74°C) before eating, for example in a stew.

blocks.p: Traditional: from a historical source, not agency-verified. The US Army survival manual (FM 21-76, 2006 copy): cut the meat with the grain into strips about 6 mm (1/4 inch) thick, hang them on a rack in a sunny place with good air flow, keep them out of reach of animals, and cover them to keep blowflies off. Let the meat dry thoroughly: properly dried meat has a dry, crisp texture and does not feel cool to the touch.

list: Its risk: there is no steady heat to stop germs, and animals, insects, dust and bacteria can get at the meat while it dries (USDA, quoted below).

What the agencies say, from Preserving food: “Sun drying is not recommended for making meat jerky, because there is no steady heat source and animals, insects, dust and bacteria can contaminate it (USDA).” The National Center for Home Food Preservation does not recommend drying meats outdoors.
End step: cook it to 165°F (74°C) before eating, for example in a stew.

blocks.p: Traditional: from a historical source, not agency-verified. The US Army survival manual (FM 21-76, 2006 copy): soak the meat thoroughly in a saltwater solution that covers it, and wash off the salt before cooking. It gives no salt strength and no time.
Traditional: from an extension source, not agency-verified. North Dakota State University Extension, corning game (corned venison):

steps: For 6 gallons (23 L) of corning liquid: 3 pounds (1.4 kg) of salt, 10 ounces (280 g) of sugar, spices (pepper, ground cloves, bay leaves, pickling spice) and curing salts, made up to 6 gallons with water (North Dakota State University Extension). Use food-grade salt with no additives such as iodine (National Center for Home Food Preservation).

Curing salts: this app gives no amounts of sodium nitrate or nitrite. A mistake with them can be a lethal dose (National Center for Home Food Preservation). Use only a commercial cure mix, by its package directions (National Center for Home Food Preservation; North Dakota State University Extension does the same for its brine cure). Without one, this app’s caution: don’t corn meat.

Put the meat in the liquid, weighted down if needed so it stays under, for 15 days. Stir the liquid and turn the meat on days 5 and 10 (North Dakota State University Extension). Use a crock or food-grade container (North Dakota State University Extension).

Cure only at 35 to 40°F (2 to 4°C): the National Center for Home Food Preservation sets that range, the upper limit to limit the growth of germs. North Dakota State University Extension calls about 38°F (3°C) ideal, and also gives extra salt for curing warmer; this app does not give that, because it would mean curing above the National Center for Home Food Preservation’s 40°F (4°C).
If the brine turns ropy, take the meat out (North Dakota State University Extension, for its brine cure).

To cook it: cover with cold water, bring it to a boil, skim off the scum, and simmer about five hours or until tender. Keep what you don’t use straight away in a cool place, refrigerated at 38°F (3°C), and cook and eat it within one week of taking it out of the liquid, or freeze it for up to one month (North Dakota State University Extension). Without that cold, no source opened for this app gives any keeping time.

list: Its risk: germs grow if the meat is too warm (National Center for Home Food Preservation sets 40°F (4°C) as the upper limit for curing for that reason), and the germ that causes botulism thrives in moist food low in salt, under 10 percent (National Center for Home Food Preservation). A curing-salt mistake can kill (National Center for Home Food Preservation).

What the agencies say: cure meat between 35°F and 40°F (2°C and 4°C); the upper limit is there to limit the growth of germs (National Center for Home Food Preservation). Curing (salting) alone does not consistently kill trichinella worms (CDC).
End step: cook it to 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part before eating, whatever the recipe says.
Canning: no procedure. Pressure canning by tested instructions is the only recommended way to can meat, and it is in Preserving food only as a warning.
Dry-cured and brine-cured whole legs (ham-style): North Dakota State University Extension’s cures take 4 to 6 weeks or more at 38°F (3°C) with curing salts. Not given here.
Cured, dried or fermented sausage: never, for the reasons in Butchering deer and small game.
Pemmican and any other method no source opened for this app teaches.
